title: Census unearthed: Population, widows and orphans in 1921
meta_description: From a lack of living space to an increase in the number of widows and orphans, newly digitised county and district level statistics from the 1921 Census show changes after World War I and the Spanish Flu pandemic.

breadcrumb.text: Census unearthed: Population, widows and orphans in 1921

lede: From a lack of living space to an increase in the number of widows and orphans, newly digitised county and district level statistics from the 1921 Census show changes after World War I and the Spanish Flu pandemic.

body.text: 12 April 2022
Just three years on from the end of World War I and in the wake of the Spanish flu pandemic, the 1921 Census took a snapshot of life in England and Wales and found a population forever changed.

For the first and only time, information was gathered on orphanhood status, offering insight into the possible effects of war and pandemic. The 1921 Census was also the first to recognise divorce as a marital condition.
The 1921 Census statistics provide more detailed information for the larger or more populous geographical areas.

As digitised tables, those relating to orphanhood and marital condition are limited to districts with a population over 50,000. While the analysis for this data has been carried out at district level, we have provided maps at county level to give better coverage of England and Wales.
Explore how areas compared with each other by using our interactive visualisations.

body.h2: More than 11% of all women in 1921 were widows
body.text: More than 11% of all women in 1921 were widows

body.h2: More than 11% of all women in 1921 were widows
body.text: The 1921 Census recorded that just over 11% of all females aged 15 and older were widows, compared with 10% of the same in the 1911 Census; a 1% increase.

body.h2: More than 11% of all women in 1921 were widows
body.text: A larger difference was evident when comparing younger, narrower age groups of females. For example, 1.3% of women aged 25 to 34 years were widowed in 1911. By 1921, that had increased to 3.2% of females in the same age group.

body.h2: More than 11% of all women in 1921 were widows
body.text: For men in 1921, the proportion was smaller, where 5% of all males aged 15 and above and 0.9% aged 20 to 39 were widowed.

body.h2: More than 11% of all women in 1921 were widows
body.text: Not all widowed spouses recorded in the census would have lost their husband or wife through war or pandemic, but for comparison, [239,000 widows and 393,000 children received a war pension in 1921 in Britain.](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0363199014548826)

body.h2: More than 11% of all women in 1921 were widows
body.text: [Around 228,000 people were estimated to have died in Britain from Spanish flu](https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/politicsandpolicy/public-memory-1918-flu/#:~:text=The%20'Spanish%20Flu'%20pandemic%20killed,Spanish%20Flu'%20was%20a%20misnomer.) a large number of them fit and healthy. [It is thought that in the UK, the virus was spread by soldiers returning home from the trenches in northern France during World War I.](https://www.historic-uk.com/HistoryUK/HistoryofBritain/The-Spanish-Flu-pandemic-of-1918/)

body.h2: Use the interactive to find out how many widows lived in your county
body.text: Looking more locally, district-level data shows the proportion of widowed spouses. Of urban areas, the highest proportion of widowed females, aged 15 and above, (15%) and aged 20 to 39 (4%) lived in metropolitan borough of Finsbury, London.

body.h2: Use the interactive to find out how many widows lived in your county
body.text: Meanwhile, the district with the lowest proportion of widowed females, was Rhondda urban district in the South Wales valleys, with 9% of women aged 15 and above.

body.h2: Use the interactive to find out how many widows lived in your county
body.text: Barrow in Furness county borough had the lowest proportion of widowed females aged 20 to 39 (2%).

body.h2: First time divorce is included in marital status
body.text: For the first time in census history, the 1921 survey included divorce and showed that 0.06% of people aged 15 and over were divorced in 1921 (16,682 people).

body.h2: First time divorce is included in marital status
body.text: The largest number of marriage dissolutions recorded by age in 1921 amounted to 2,860 for people aged between 35 and 39 years.

body.h2: First time divorce is included in marital status
body.text: [Divorce was still relatively rare in England and Wales in 1921, and often a source of stigma and shame for those involved.](https://www.parliament.uk/business/publications/research/olympic-britain/housing-and-home-life/split-pairs/) It was also largely a preserve of those who could afford it.

body.h2: First time divorce is included in marital status
body.text: A raft of legislation followed in 1921 which put males and females on a more equal footing by providing further grounds for divorce other than adultery or violence.

body.h2: First time divorce is included in marital status
body.text: [While there was a slight increase in divorces in the late 1920s, dramatic increases were](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/datasets/vitalstatisticspopulationandhealthreferencetables) not seen until the mid to late 1940s.

body.h2: First time divorce is included in marital status
body.text: By the [1961 Census](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/housing/articles/censusunearthedexplore50yearsofchangefrom1961/2021-08-09) 0.8% of people aged 16 years and over were divorced (of marriageable age) and 9% were divorced or in a legally dissolved civil partnership by the 2011 Census.

body.h2: Orphans counted in the census for the first and only time
body.text: Orphans counted in the census for the first and only time

body.h2: Orphans counted in the census for the first and only time
body.text: Details of orphanhood and dependency status was vital in a post-pandemic and post-conflict 1921. It helped prepare the financial framework of the Widows, Orphans and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act, 1925.

body.h2: Orphans counted in the census for the first and only time
body.text: This would have been the first and only time that questions about orphanhood status were asked about children aged 14 and under in the 1921 Census.

body.h2: Orphans counted in the census for the first and only time
body.text: That information, laid bare in black and white on the census form, showed for the first time how many orphans there were in England and Wales.

body.h2: Orphans counted in the census for the first and only time
body.text: The two cold words on the census form, “father dead”, meant life without the “head of the family” for 730,845 children, as recorded in the 1921 Census. Their absence would leave a lasting legacy for generations to come.

body.h2: Orphans counted in the census for the first and only time
body.text: The number of children recorded as “mother dead” was 261,094, almost three times fewer than those without a father. Those who lost both parents numbered 55,245.

body.h2: Orphans counted in the census for the first and only time
body.text: The letters after district place names are part of their description – a county borough (CB), for example, is a distinct area from an urban district (UD) or a metropolitan area (ME).

body.h2: Orphans counted in the census for the first and only time
body.text: Of urban areas, Finsbury Metropolitan Borough in London had the highest percentage of fatherless children aged 14 and under (10%), while Hastings county borough in East Sussex and Bury county borough in Lancashire each had just under 10%. There was also a cluster of other London districts which had a high percentage of children whose father had died.

body.h2: Orphans counted in the census for the first and only time
body.text: Aberdare urban district, a mining town in South Wales, had the highest percentage (3%) of children aged 14 years and below whose mothers had died. Merthyr Tydfil county borough in South Wales, Oldham county borough in Lancashire, and Sunderland county borough, all had around 3%.

body.h2: Orphans counted in the census for the first and only time
body.text: The urban district of Enfield, London was the district with the highest percentage (1%) of children aged 14 years and below where both parents had died. There were two more London urban districts in this position; Hendon and Ilford.

body.h2: Female population of England and Wales outnumbered males in 1921 across all ages
body.text: Female population of England and Wales outnumbered males in 1921 across all ages

body.h2: Female population of England and Wales outnumbered males in 1921 across all ages
body.text: In 1921, the number of females in England and Wales outnumbered males by 19.8 million to 18 million respectively across all ages. This compares with 18.6 million females and 17.4 million males in 1911.

body.h2: Female population of England and Wales outnumbered males in 1921 across all ages
body.text: The imbalance between males and females in 1921 was most pronounced among those in their 20s and 30s.

body.h2: Female population of England and Wales outnumbered males in 1921 across all ages
body.text: During the first two decades of the 20th century, [government schemes existed to encourage ‘surplus women’ to emigrate to other parts of what was then the British Empire, to try and redress the imbalance].[7]

body.h2: Female population of England and Wales outnumbered males in 1921 across all ages
body.text: This imbalance in the number of females to men revealed, in unrounded figures, that in 1921 there was 1.1 female for every 1 male, compared to 1.07 women to every 1 male in 1911.

body.h2: Females stay coastal while males are in military barracks
body.text: Females stay coastal while males are in military barracks

body.h2: Females stay coastal while males are in military barracks
body.text: Nine out of the 10 districts with the highest percentage of females are coastal.

body.h2: Females stay coastal while males are in military barracks
body.text: But rather than this being an increase in the number of females, this information could be more about the lack of males. On census night, anyone at sea, such as fishermen or members of the merchant navy, who did not arrive in port the following morning, would not be included in the census count.

body.h2: Females stay coastal while males are in military barracks
body.text: The census showed most districts which included the highest proportion of males were also home to institutions such as military or naval barracks, or prisons.

body.h2: Females stay coastal while males are in military barracks
body.text: For example, Amesbury rural district in Wiltshire, had the second highest percentage point difference between males and females (29pp) on census night, with 65% males and 35% females. Amesbury is also the location of a military barracks in which there were 5,308 males and 972 females making 5.5 males for every female within the barracks.

body.h2: Females stay coastal while males are in military barracks
body.text: Portland urban district in Dorset saw a 24 percentage point difference in males compared to females.

body.h2: Females stay coastal while males are in military barracks
body.text: There were 2,703 males in naval barracks, naval hospitals or Royal Navy ships on census night, compared with 100 females. That made 27 males for every female.

body.h2: Females stay coastal while males are in military barracks
body.text: While members of the Armed Forces serving overseas were included in the census, there were some [exceptions from the count.](https://search.findmypast.co.uk/search-world-records/1921-census-of-england-and-wales)

body.h2: How the population changed in your area between 1911 and 1921
body.text: Given that the 1921 Census was conducted during holiday season in June, following a three-month postponement, it’s likely that the population of popular holiday destinations such as Blackpool was larger in 1921 than it was in 1911.

body.h2: How the population changed in your area between 1911 and 1921
body.text: Blackpool county borough saw the second largest population percentage point increase between the 1911 and 1921 Census, as a proportion of England and Wales (0.09%).

body.h2: How the population changed in your area between 1911 and 1921
body.text: Two other seaside locations were also among the 10 places which saw the largest population percentage point increase on census night, Southend on Sea county borough and Margate municipal borough.

body.h2: How the population changed in your area between 1911 and 1921
body.text: The Census General Report was very confident that there was a known effect on holiday resorts, stating there was 'no doubt' that the 'periodical summer movement' had caused a greater divergence of resident and counted populations than if the census had been taken in April.

body.h2: How the population changed in your area between 1911 and 1921
body.text: The City of Birmingham county borough experienced the highest percentage point change as a proportion of the population of England and Wales between 1911 and 1921, which was 0.1%. This was a time of rapid urbanisation, which could explain the change.

body.h2: How the population changed in your area between 1911 and 1921
body.text: London districts made up seven out of 10 places with the largest population percentage point decrease between 1911 and 1921. Stepney metropolitan borough saw the greatest percentage point decrease.

body.h2: Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes
body.text: Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes

body.h2: Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes
body.text: The 1921 Census collected information on how many rooms people had and how many people lived in their home.

body.h2: Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes
body.text: This information was used to calculate density of occupation in terms of rooms per person.

body.h2: Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes
body.text: The rooms counted were the usual living rooms, including bedrooms and kitchens but excluding sculleries, landings, lobbies, closets, bathrooms, or any warehouse, office or shop rooms.

Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes
body.title: Rooms per person

body.h2: Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes
body.text: [Data for 1921 on rooms per person (XLSX, 69KB)](/visualisations/dvc1866/roomsperperson/data/datadownload.xlsx)

body.h2: Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes
body.text: Hebburn urban district in the county of Durham, had the least amount of living space, with just 0.59 rooms per person. This district also saw an increase in population between 1911 and 1921, alongside seven out of the 10 districts with the least living space.

body.h2: Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes
body.text: The only non-Northern district among those with the least number of rooms per person was Shoreditch metropolitan borough in London, with 0.65 rooms per person.

body.h2: Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes
body.text: Shoreditch also had fewer people there on census night as a proportion of the population of England and Wales, than in 1911, a percentage point drop of 0.03%.

body.h2: Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes
body.text: Shoreditch saw both a reduction in population and was one of the top 10 places with the least amount of living space. Despite the reduction in population, the area was still in the top 10 for rooms per person, suggesting how little space people had to live in.

body.h2: Districts in the Northern Counties had a large share of densely occupied homes
body.text: Districts with the most number of rooms per person were primarily coastal or rural; Woodhall Spa urban district in Lincolnshire had the most space, with 1.82 rooms per person.
